summary: Redwood AE + SE (Jordan, Priya) walked BrightPath through Redwood Optimize recommendations focusing on batching and prefix/KV cache strategies and how they map to cost models. BrightPath is evaluating a pilot to reduce token cost for their analytics summarization pipelines while keeping p95 latency under 600ms. Action items include sharing pricing, sample traces, and scheduling a pilot kickoff.
topics: batching guidance (dynamic vs fixed, batch size tradeoffs)
prefix vs KV cache recommendations for conversational summarization workloads
cost model walkthrough (tokens, batches, GPU utilisation, quantization impact)
pilot scope: benchmarks and success criteria
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Okay, good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. This is Jordan from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Priya our SE. How are you folks doing?

[00:08] Michael Torres: Hey Jordan, doing well, thanks. Sara and Rahul are on as well. We got about an hour set aside — excited to see the Optimize recommendations.

[00:15] Sara Lee: Yep hi all, excited. We're mainly interested in reducing token cost for our nightly summarization and keeping interactive query latency tight.

[00:25] Priya Desai: Great, we'll try to focus on concrete recs — batching policies, caching patterns (prefix vs K V cache), and then a simple cost model so you can compare hosted vs dedicated. Quick note: I'll reference the benchmark sheet and deck — I'll drop links in the follow-up.

[00:38] Rahul Gupta: Quick question on scope: our pipeline is 70% short queries (<= 128 tokens) and 30% long summaries (~1,500 tokens). We care about p95 latency under 600ms for the interactive bits.

[00:50] Priya Desai: That mix matters a lot — thanks Rahul. For that distribution we usually recommend hybrid batching where short queries go through a low-latency path with smaller batch windows and long summaries are batched more aggressively or run on dedicated workers to avoid impacting p95.

[01:10] Jordan Kim: Before we dive deep — are you leaning hosted API or Dedicated? That affects the tradeoffs.

[01:18] Michael Torres: We're evaluating both. Hosted first for speed; Dedicated if unit cost doesn't meet targets or we need isolation. Also compliance people want VPC options in the long run.

[01:28] Priya Desai: Totally makes sense. We'll show numbers for both.

[02:05] Priya Desai: Okay slide 3 — batching basics. Two knobs: batch window (how long server waits to fill a batch) and max batch size. For latency-sensitive short queries set batch window low (5-20ms) and smaller max batch size. For throughput-y long jobs you can increase window to 50-200ms and larger batch sizes to improve GPU utilization. There is also continuous batching in our runtime which can help lower queuing jitter.

[03:00] Sara Lee: When you say batch window 20ms, is that client-controlled or server?

[03:06] Priya Desai: Both. You can set client-side hints and our router honors them (best-effort) — Dedicated allows more control and stricter SLOs for batching behavior.

[03:32] Priya Desai: Now onto prefix and KV cache. For your summarization use case, you said you have a long context where the prefix (system prompt + user history) is stable across many requests — that's prime for prefix caching.

[03:50] Rahul Gupta: Could you clarify prefix vs KV cache? I thought prefix caching was the same as K V.

[03:56] Priya Desai: Common confusion. Prefix cache stores entire prompt prefixes and their intermediate KV states for reuse when the next request uses the same prefix. KV cache is more fine-grained — it stores key/value pairs for transformer layers for reuse across similar sequences. Practically, prefix cache is simpler and higher-hit-rate when you have repeated templates; KV cache is better for conversational flows where only recent tokens vary. In our runtime we support both; you can layer them.

[04:30] Michael Torres: Our summarization job uses a consistent system prompt with per-record text. So prefix cache sounds useful.

[04:36] Priya Desai: Exactly. If the system prompt + template is stable you can cache the prefix KVs once per template and save multiple forward passes. In the deck I dropped an example where we saw up to 3x token compute reduction on template-heavy workloads. Note: transcription error earlier — some decks say "K V cash" in the example sheet, ignore that.

[05:10] Sara Lee: Nice. How does this change the cost model?

[05:16] Priya Desai: Two ways: fewer tokens processed per request (so fewer GPU ops) and higher effective throughput (more requests per second for same GPU). On the sheet we model per-token cost, batch efficiency, and cache hit rate. Let me walk through a simple example: baseline no-cache, avg tokens per request 1,200, and we assume 30 requests/sec -> X tokens/sec -> GPU utilization Y. With prefix cache and a 70% hit rate, you only compute the variable suffix ~30% of the time, cutting effective tokens by roughly 2.3x in that example.

[06:05] Rahul Gupta: Is hit rate realistic? Our records have some variability.

[06:09] Priya Desai: Hit rate depends on template count and variability. If you have 20 templates used across requests and one template accounts for 50% of traffic, you'll get better than uniform distribution. For pilots we ask customers to provide request traces so we can estimate realistic hit rates — that's one of the next steps.

[06:35] Jordan Kim: On the pricing side, hosted is per-token and we show how caching reduces billable tokens; Dedicated is capacity-based so caching improves throughput and can delay scale-ups, affecting committed capacity choices.

[07:02] Michael Torres: Any caveats? Does caching increase memory usage on the serving nodes?

[07:07] Priya Desai: Yes — caching KV states consumes GPU memory. There's a tradeoff: higher cache hit rate reduces compute but increases memory usage. We surface this in Redwood Optimize recommendations — we give recommended cache sizes and eviction policies based on your template cardinality.

[07:30] Priya Desai: Also quantization interacts — some quantized kernels have smaller KV sizes and different perf. We include quantization impact in the cost model.

[08:00] Sara Lee: Can you show the worked cost example for our numbers?

[08:05] Priya Desai: Sure. I'll walk through the spreadsheet row. Baseline: 1,500 tokens avg for long jobs, 128 tokens for short. Mix 70/30. Hosted per-token price assumed $0.0004 per token (placeholder, we'll send updated hosted rates). Baseline monthly tokens ~ Z (we're showing relative numbers). With prefix cache at 60% hit rate you get ~1.7x effective reduction in token compute for long jobs. With batching on the long jobs at batch size 16 you get another 20-30% improvement in GPU throughput. Combined you can see cost per request drop ~2.5x in that model.

[09:20] Michael Torres: That's promising. How do you avoid increased latency for short queries if batch windows are bigger for long jobs?

[09:28] Priya Desai: Router policy. We tag short query routes with low-latency policy and route them to nodes with low batch windows. For long summaries either run on a separate pool or allow batching policies that prioritize throughput. For Dedicated, you can reserve separate pools; for Hosted we do tenant-aware routing to avoid head-of-line issues.

[10:02] Rahul Gupta: Is there any real-world example at scale that shows p95 staying under target while using these optimizations?

[10:09] Priya Desai: Yes — in a reference customer in ad tech we maintained p95 under 450ms for short queries while long jobs hit p99s higher but were routed to different pools. We can share anonymized traces.

[10:25] Jordan Kim: Competitors sometimes advertise batching but not the routing policy or cache layer — that's where Redwood's runtime and Optimize tooling show ROI.

[10:40] Sara Lee: Security note — our compliance team will ask about KMS and audit logs. How does caching interact with encryption?

[10:48] Priya Desai: Good question. KV/prefix caches are stored encrypted at rest on the GPU node disk (if spilled) and in-memory are protected; for Private/VPC we can integrate with your KMS/HSM or use Redwood-managed KMS if you choose. Audit logs track cache ops, evictions, and access — we can include that in the pilot scope.

[11:20] Michael Torres: Great. On Dedicated, what's the typical commit level to make it cost-effective?

[11:26] Jordan Kim: It varies by workload. For this mix, and given your traffic projection, the model sheet suggests ~4-6 reserved GPUs to start for Dedicated to be worthwhile versus hosted, assuming 60% average utilization. That assumes you can tolerate some burst and/or scale policies. We'll provide a tailored calc once you share traces.

[12:02] Priya Desai: Quick demo time — I'm going to share my screen and show the Optimize console. (brief pause) Here is the per-route cost breakdown: tokens, batch efficiency, average batch size, cache hit rate. You can click into a route and get suggestions: "lower batch window" or "enable prefix cache" with an estimated token savings.

[13:00] Priya Desai: Example: route /summaries-1 shows average batch size 4, batch efficiency 0.45; we recommend increasing max batch to 16 for the worker pool and enabling prefix cache for templates 1,2,3. Estimated savings ~38% on token compute.

[13:30] Sara Lee: How do we instrument to collect the metrics?

[13:34] Priya Desai: Out-of-the-box SDKs emit route and token metrics. For Private we ship an agent you can run; for Hosted it’s server-side. We can also ingest your Prometheus traces.

[14:10] Rahul Gupta: For our pilot we want to run a 2-week benchmark. What's typical?

[14:15] Priya Desai: Two weeks gives a good view of variability; at minimum 3-5 days with weekday/weekend splits. We'll run synthetic and replayed traces. The outcome: hit rates, p95, cost per 10k requests, and guidance on Dedicated sizing.

[15:00] Michael Torres: Could you briefly show the eviction policy options?

[15:05] Priya Desai: Sure. LRU is default. We support TTL-based eviction, size-based eviction, and application-driven invalidation (via API). For template-heavy workloads TTL plus LRU works well. For conversations you'd want short TTL and smaller KV cache to avoid memory pressure.

[16:00] Sara Lee: Any gotchas with quantized models (like 4-bit) and caching?

[16:07] Priya Desai: Some quantized kernels change KV storage format and might slightly change memory footprint, but Redwood's runtime normalizes those differences and we account for them in the model. There can be minor accuracy/quality tradeoffs with aggressive quantization; Optimize flags potential quality regressions in evaluation runs.

[17:05] Rahul Gupta: On the topic of quality monitoring, can we tie regressions back to specific prompts or rollout changes?

[17:12] Priya Desai: Yes. The evals integration in Console ties prompt sets to metrics; if quality drops after a model swap or quantization change we send alerts and you can auto-roll back.

[18:00] Jordan Kim: Quick interruption — Michael, are there internal stakeholders for security/compliance we should loop in before pilot?

[18:07] Michael Torres: Yes, I'll loop in Legal and Infosec — Ken from Security and Priya (not your Priya) from Legal.

[18:15] Jordan Kim: Perfect; we'll include our security pack (SOC2 docs, data flow diagrams).

[19:00] Priya Desai: Back to the cost model: one more slide showing sensitivity analysis — cache hit rate (x-axis) vs cost reduction (y-axis). For your mix, the knee is around 40-60% hit rate for meaningful infra impact.

[19:35] Sara Lee: If we enable prefix caching, do we need to change our prompt templates?

[19:41] Priya Desai: Minimal changes — usually standardize system prompts and move any constant instructions into the prefix so the runtime can reuse KV states. We can help with a short checklist.

[20:10] Michael Torres: Let's talk numbers. If we assume 60% cache hit, what is the monthly savings on hosted at our projected volume?

[20:17] Priya Desai: On the sheet, 60% hit with your mix reduces estimated token spend by ~55%, effectively halving your hosted bill (rough numbers; we'll send exact rows). If you then go Dedicated, you see marginal unit cost reductions depending on how many GPUs you reserve. The spreadsheet includes break-even curves.

[21:05] Rahul Gupta: Any instrumentation needed for the KV cache warm-up?

[21:10] Priya Desai: Warm-up can be done via a pre-warm job that populates popular prefixes during deploys; we recommend running that as part of rollout. We'll provide a script template.

[22:00] Jordan Kim: Switching to pilot logistics — expected deliverables: baseline replayed run, enable caching, run batched long jobs, measure p95/p99, report cost delta, and recommendations for Dedicated sizing. Does that sound right?

[22:12] Michael Torres: Yes. Also include a short appendix on security and data residency.

[22:20] Priya Desai: Will do. We'll also record tests with and without quantization to compare quality.

[23:00] Sara Lee: A customer question — are there licensing or IP implications for caching customer data?

[23:06] Priya Desai: Prefix/KV caches only store model intermediate states, not raw customer PII as raw text — still, we treat them as sensitive artifacts and encrypt/expire them. We'll document that in the security pack.

[24:00] Michael Torres: Any limitations on template count for caching?

[24:05] Priya Desai: Memory is the main limiter. If you have thousands of templates you can tier them or use TTLs; Optimize will recommend groupings.

[25:00] Jordan Kim: Quick note on competitors — some offer caching layers but struggle with integrated routing and cost transparency, which is where Redwood Optimize helps consolidate recommendations and show dollar impact.

[26:10] Rahul Gupta: About eviction again — if we purge a prefix in the middle of active requests could it cause errors?

[26:16] Priya Desai: No errors; eviction affects cache hit rate only. Requests falling back will compute full forward pass; we handle in-flight consistency.

[27:00] Sara Lee: Are there built-in dashboards for these metrics?

[27:05] Priya Desai: Yes per-route dashboards, batch histograms, and cache heatmaps. We can also export to your analytics stack.

[28:00] Michael Torres: Ok good. Let's close with concrete next steps. Jordan?

[28:06] Jordan Kim: We'll send the pricing and the Optimize deck + benchmark sheet by Monday. Priya will include a pilot plan. Michael we'll need the request traces and the stakeholders for security review.

[28:22] Michael Torres: Sounds good. Any final questions?

[28:30] Sara Lee: Just one — how long to stand up a pilot on Hosted vs Dedicated?

[28:36] Priya Desai: Hosted pilot can start within 2-3 days; Dedicated pilot depends on carve-out and reserved capacity but minimal Dedicated proof-of-concept can run within 7-14 days if you're ready to commit.

[29:00] Rahul Gupta: What's the rollback story if quality drops?

[29:04] Priya Desai: Rollback is trivial via Console — model or quantization profile rollback plus audit trail. We support auto-rollback triggers on eval thresholds.

[30:00] Jordan Kim: Okay we'll recap in the follow-up email and include the sheet link and next steps. Thanks everyone.

[30:08] Michael Torres: Thanks Jordan, Priya — appreciate it. We'll get the traces over.

[30:15] Sara Lee: Thanks team.

[30:20] (call ends)
